pages.x: In 1547 Ivan IV, grand prince of Moscow, was crowned the first tsar of all Russia, a title taken from Caesar. To the east lay the Tatar khanates, heirs of the Golden Horde that had once ruled the Russians.

In 1552 Ivan besieged Kazan, on the Volga, with some 150,000 men. His engineers dug tunnels under the walls and blew them open with gunpowder, and the city was stormed and its men killed. Astrakhan fell in 1556, and the whole Volga was Russian.

To give thanks, Ivan built a cathedral on Red Square with nine chapels under bright onion domes. A legend says he blinded its architects so they could never build anything as beautiful again. It is almost certainly untrue.

Ivan grew cruel and suspicious. His black-robed guards, the oprichniki, terrorised the land and in 1570 massacred thousands in Novgorod. In 1581, in a rage, he struck his own son and heir with his staff and killed him.

In 1582 a Cossack chief, Yermak, paid by the Stroganov merchants, crossed the Urals with about 800 men and took Isker, capital of the khanate of Sibir. He drowned in a river in 1585, weighed down, the story goes, by armour the tsar had given him.
Cossacks and fur trappers pushed east along the great rivers, building wooden forts as they went. In 1639 they reached the Pacific. The furs of Siberia, sable above all, made the tsars rich.

The conquests turned Muscovy into a vast empire of many peoples and faiths that reached the Pacific within a century. Russia is still the largest country on Earth, and Siberia makes up three quarters of it.
